column6: Against the page's offered reminder and non-coercive teacher, Hebrews warns hearers not to refuse the one speaking; its contrast between an earthly warning and a heavenly address makes rejection of a delivered warning liable to judgment.
The commentary calls the reminder beneficial and contrasts guidance with self-directed avoidance; Isaiah has YHWH teach his people for their profit and lead them in the way they should go.
Isaiah says attention to the commandments would have made peace like a river; this adds the foregone good to the commentary's claim that the wretched person treats benefit as harm.
YHWH offers salvation in returning and rest and strength in quietness and trust, then says the hearers were unwilling; it closely forms the page's offered guidance and personally chosen refusal.

column5: a word saying walk this way
column6: When the people turn right or left, their ears hear a word behind them saying this is the way and to walk in it; this is a precise alternative to passing the available reminder by on the road.
Isaiah's commission tells the audience to keep hearing and seeing without understanding or perceiving, a direct prophetic scene of words and signs present yet unreceived.

column5: divinely dulled heart, ears, and eyes
column6: Isaiah is commanded to make heart dull, ears heavy, and eyes blind; the page instead narrates avoidance as the person's action and blindness as a later consequence, so the agency and sequence form a material counter-reading.
Jesus asks disciples whether they have eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear, and whether they do not remember; it closely joins the page's forgotten signs with its final blindness.
Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself before YHWH, a direct biblical expression of the page's invitation to Pharaoh to purify himself and his refusal.
After relief from the plague Pharaoh sins again and makes his heart heavy; this explicit self-hardening is a distinct counterpart to the page's self-directed turning from the warning.

column5: desire as god and earthly mind
column6: The page says the self-directed person makes desire into an idol; Paul describes people whose god is their belly, whose end is destruction, and whose minds are set on earthly things.

column5: deliberate sin after knowledge of truth
column6: Hebrews describes deliberate persistence in sin after receiving knowledge of the truth; it makes received revelation, rather than lack of exposure, the setting for culpable rejection.
The fearful expectation of judgment and fire consuming adversaries gives the previous verse's rejection a concrete punitive outcome alongside the commentary's great fire.
Jesus wishes to gather Jerusalem's children but says they were unwilling; it gives an offer of protection that does not coerce its addressees, like the page's reminder.

The page treats junub as temporary distance from prayer ended by washing; Leviticus requires a man with seminal emission to wash his whole body and remain unclean until evening, a close ritual analogue with a differently framed sacred boundary.

Leviticus orders Israel to be kept separate from impurity lest it defile the tabernacle and bring death; it supplies the cultic-boundary dimension beside the page's temporary washing before return to prayer.
The page reads its side-language as regret over what was neglected in God's nearness; the psalmist calls the nearness of God his good, giving that spatial claim a positive biblical pole.

column5: working salvation with fear and trembling
column6: The commentary treats remembering, avoidance, and purification as personally enacted forms and joins purification to fear; Paul commands believers to work out salvation with fear and trembling.

column5: blind seeker restored and following the way
column6: Unlike the page's unnamed blind visitor, Mark's Bartimaeus receives sight and follows Jesus on the way; it is an indirect but specific counterpart to the blind person who comes toward the teacher rather than avoiding the offered guidance.
